standard_text: Understand the formulas for area and circumference of a circle and use them to solve real-world and other mathematical problems; give an informal derivation of the relationship between circumference and area of a circle.

progression.narrative: This standard asks students to find the circumference and area of circles, work backwards from a given circumference or area to a radius or diameter, and explain how the two formulas relate. The on-grade work runs from the two forward formulas through the reverse problems to real contexts where the student must pick the right formula for the situation. Students who struggle here usually cannot yet handle any measurement formula, not just the circle ones: perimeter and area are still fuzzy ideas rather than distance around and squares covering. Intervention should start with the grade 3 to 5 basics, perimeter as adding side lengths and area as rows of unit squares, then rebuild the grade 6 skills of finding areas by decomposing shapes and evaluating a formula by substitution, and only then return to circles.

steps.rationale: The first forward formula, C = 2πr = πd, a single multiplication. It is where the radius-versus-diameter trap first appears: πd uses the diameter, 2πr uses the radius.
The second forward formula, A = πr², adds the squaring step and a second, costlier place for the diameter-as-radius error — using the diameter quadruples the answer.
Reverses circumference with a single division. Students who can go forward must also recover a radius or diameter from a given circumference — without stopping at the diameter.
Reverses area, which needs BOTH a division by π and a square root. It earns its own step because the square root is the move students skip.
The At-proficiency application: the student must choose the right formula for a context (fence = circumference, cover = area) and handle the radius or diameter the story gives.
The Above-proficiency informal derivation: doubling the radius doubles the circumference but quadruples the area, showing the student reasons about the formulas rather than just plugging in.

skills.name: Find the perimeter of a rectangle by adding side lengths

prerequisite_skill.description: Find the distance around a rectangle by adding all four side lengths.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: A rectangle is 5 cm long and 3 cm wide. What is its perimeter?

skills.i_do_script: Perimeter is the walk around the outside of a shape. Watch: this rectangle on grid paper is 5 units long and 3 units wide. I put my pencil at a corner and walk the edge, counting unit steps: 5 along the top, 3 down the side, 5 along the bottom, 3 back up. That is 5 + 3 + 5 + 3 = 16 units all the way around. A rectangle always has two matching lengths and two matching widths, so I add all four sides, not just the two I can see numbers on.

canonical_error.pattern: Adds only the two labeled sides instead of all four
canonical_error.example: For a 5 by 3 rectangle, writes 5 + 3 = 8 instead of 5 + 3 + 5 + 3 = 16
canonical_error.why: The student adds the numbers printed on the picture and stops. A rectangle has four sides; the unlabeled length and width match the labeled ones and must be counted in the walk around.

skills.item_template: A rectangle or square with whole-number side lengths. Student finds the perimeter by adding all side lengths. Short response fluency bank.

sample_items.stem: A rectangle is 5 cm long and 3 cm wide. What is its perimeter?
A rectangle is 6 in. long and 4 in. wide. What is its perimeter?
A square has sides of 7 ft. What is its perimeter?
A rectangle is 8 m long and 3 m wide. What is its perimeter?
A rectangle is 10 cm long and 5 cm wide. What is its perimeter?
A rectangle has sides of 4 in., 6 in., 4 in., and 6 in. What is its perimeter?
A rectangle is 9 ft long and 2 ft wide. What is its perimeter?
A square has sides of 5 m. What is its perimeter?

redirect_script.stop: Did you walk all the way around the shape?
redirect_script.prompt: Trace the edge with your finger and count every side as you pass it. A rectangle has four sides: two lengths and two widths. Add all four numbers, not just the two written on the picture.
redirect_script.praise: You counted every side of the walk around, that is perimeter.

vocabulary.definition: The distance all the way around the outside of a shape.
How long one edge of a shape is.

next_steps.if_fail: Review grade 3 perimeter on grid paper: trace a shape's edge and count unit steps all the way around.

worked_example_script.text: Draw a 5 by 3 rectangle on grid paper. Start a pencil at one corner and mark unit steps along the edge as you walk around.
How many steps along the top? Down the side? Do we stop there, or keep walking?
Keep walking until you are back where you started: 5 + 3 + 5 + 3 = 16 steps. The perimeter is 16 units, the whole trip around.
If a student answers 8, ask them to finish the walk: you are only halfway around the rectangle.
Your turn: walk around a 6 by 2 rectangle. What is the perimeter?

skills.name: Find the area of a rectangle by counting rows of unit squares

prerequisite_skill.description: Find the area of a rectangle by counting the unit squares that cover it, organized as equal rows.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: A rectangle is 4 squares wide and 3 squares tall. How many unit squares cover it?

skills.i_do_script: Area is how many unit squares it takes to cover a shape with no gaps. Watch: this rectangle is 4 squares wide and 3 squares tall. Instead of counting the squares one at a time, I see rows: each row holds 4 squares, and there are 3 rows. That is 4 + 4 + 4, or 3 rows of 4, which is 12 squares. Area counts the squares INSIDE the shape, so the answer is 12 square units, not a distance around.

canonical_error.pattern: Adds the side lengths instead of counting the covering squares, confusing area with perimeter
canonical_error.example: For a 4 by 3 rectangle, writes 4 + 3 + 4 + 3 = 14 squares instead of 4 x 3 = 12
canonical_error.why: The student measures the trip around the edge instead of the squares covering the inside. Perimeter is a walk around; area is a count of the squares that fill the shape.

skills.item_template: A rectangle or square described by its width and height in unit squares. Student finds the area as rows of unit squares. Short response fluency bank.

sample_items.stem: A rectangle is 4 squares wide and 3 squares tall. What is its area?
A rectangle is 5 squares wide and 2 squares tall. What is its area?
A rectangle is 6 squares wide and 4 squares tall. What is its area?
A rectangle is 7 squares wide and 3 squares tall. What is its area?
A square is 5 squares on each side. What is its area?
A rectangle is 8 squares wide and 2 squares tall. What is its area?
A rectangle is 9 squares wide and 4 squares tall. What is its area?
A rectangle is 10 squares wide and 6 squares tall. What is its area?

redirect_script.stop: Are you counting the squares inside, or the steps around the edge?
redirect_script.prompt: Shade one full row and count its squares. Then count how many rows there are. Rows of squares cover the inside; that count is the area.
redirect_script.praise: You counted rows of squares covering the shape, that is exactly what area means.

vocabulary.definition: The number of unit squares that cover a shape with no gaps or overlaps.
A line of unit squares going across the shape; equal rows make area quick to count.

next_steps.if_fail: Review grade 3 area by tiling: cover small rectangles with square tiles and count them.

worked_example_script.text: Draw a 4 by 3 rectangle on grid paper. Shade the top row of 4 squares in one color.
How many squares are in one row? How many rows fill the rectangle?
Each row holds 4 squares and there are 3 rows: 4 + 4 + 4 = 12. The area is 12 square units, the squares covering the inside.
If a student answers 14, they added the sides like a walk around. Point inside the shape: area counts the covering squares, not the edge.
Your turn: a rectangle is 6 squares wide and 2 squares tall. What is its area?

skills.name: Find the area of triangles and composite figures by decomposing

prerequisite_skill.description: Find the area of a triangle as half a rectangle, and the area of a composite figure by splitting it into rectangles and triangles.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: A triangle has a base of 6 cm and a height of 4 cm. What is its area?

skills.i_do_script: Every triangle is half of a rectangle. Watch: draw a 6 by 4 rectangle and cut it along a diagonal. The rectangle's area is 6 x 4 = 24, and each triangle is exactly half, so the triangle's area is 24 / 2 = 12 square cm. That is why the rule is base times height, then divide by 2. For a composite figure, I split it into rectangles and triangles I know, find each piece's area, and add the pieces.

canonical_error.pattern: Forgets to halve, using base times height as the area of a triangle
canonical_error.example: For a triangle with base 6 and height 4, writes 6 x 4 = 24 instead of 24 / 2 = 12
canonical_error.why: Base times height gives the FULL rectangle the triangle sits in. The triangle is only half that rectangle, so the product must be divided by 2.

skills.item_template: A triangle with a given base and height, a parallelogram, or a composite figure built from rectangles and triangles with whole-number dimensions. Student finds the area. Numeric response.

sample_items.stem: A triangle has a base of 6 cm and a height of 4 cm. What is its area?
A triangle has a base of 10 in. and a height of 3 in. What is its area?
A triangle has a base of 8 m and a height of 5 m. What is its area?
An L-shaped figure is made of an 8 by 4 rectangle and a 3 by 2 rectangle. What is its total area?
A triangle has a base of 7 ft and a height of 4 ft. What is its area?
A parallelogram has a base of 6 cm and a height of 3 cm. What is its area?
A figure is made of a 4 by 4 square and a triangle with base 4 and height 3. What is its total area?
A triangle has a base of 12 cm and a height of 5 cm. What is its area?

redirect_script.stop: Is your answer the triangle, or the whole rectangle it sits in?
redirect_script.prompt: Draw the rectangle around the triangle. Base times height fills that whole rectangle, and the triangle is only half of it. Multiply, then divide by 2.
redirect_script.praise: You halved the rectangle, that is exactly where the triangle rule comes from.

vocabulary.definition: The side of a triangle or parallelogram you measure along the bottom.
The straight up-and-down distance from the base to the opposite point or side.
A shape built from simpler shapes like rectangles and triangles.

worked_example_script.text: Draw a 6 by 4 rectangle on grid paper and cut it along one diagonal into two triangles.
What is the rectangle's area? Are the two triangles the same size?
The rectangle holds 6 x 4 = 24 squares, and the diagonal splits it into two equal triangles, so each triangle is 24 / 2 = 12 square units.
If a student says 24, ask them to shade just the triangle: does it cover the whole rectangle, or half?
Your turn: a triangle has a base of 10 and a height of 6. What is its area?

practice_problems.stem: A rectangle is 6 m long and 3 m wide. What is its area?
A triangle has a base of 4 cm and a height of 6 cm. What is its area?
A triangle has a base of 10 in. and a height of 7 in. What is its area?
A parallelogram has a base of 8 cm and a height of 5 cm. What is its area?
An L-shaped figure is made of a 5 by 4 rectangle and a 3 by 2 rectangle. What is its total area?
A triangle has a base of 9 ft and a height of 4 ft. What is its area?
A figure is made of a 6 by 6 square with a triangle of base 6 and height 4 on top. What is its total area?
Leo found the area of a triangle with base 8 cm and height 5 cm. Find his mistake and fix it.
practice_problems.answer: He found the full rectangle, not the triangle. A triangle is half: 8 x 5 = 40, then 40 / 2 = 20 sq cm.

activities.title: Cut the Rectangle in Half
activities.instructions:
1. Each pair draws a 6 by 4 rectangle on grid paper and writes its area (24).
2. Cut the rectangle along a diagonal and stack the two triangles to show they match.
3. Glue one triangle down and write its area as half the rectangle: 24 / 2 = 12.
4. Repeat with an 8 by 5 rectangle.
5. Say each time: base times height fills the rectangle, the triangle is half.

activities.title: Shape to Area Match-Up
materials: Card deck: one card per figure, one card per area
activities.instructions:
1. Spread the cards face up.
2. Match each figure card to its area card.
3. To claim a match, say whether you halved (triangle) or added pieces (composite).
4. Two decoy area cards forgot to halve a triangle; set them aside and explain the error.

strategy_links.why: Physically cutting a rectangle into two matching triangles shows why the formula halves before the rule is named.
The forgot-to-halve error is a stable single-step mistake, ideal for find-and-fix work.
Thinking aloud 'rectangle first, then half' models the order students collapse.

questioning_prompts: What rectangle does this triangle sit inside?
Did you multiply base times height? What does that number cover?
Why do we divide by 2 for a triangle but not for a rectangle?
How could you split this composite figure into shapes you know?
What units does area use here?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student reports base times height as a triangle's area.
misconception_redirects.say: Draw the rectangle around the triangle. Your number fills the whole rectangle; shade the triangle and see it is only half. Divide by 2.
misconception_redirects.praise: You halved the rectangle, so your triangle area is true.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student uses a slanted side as the height.
misconception_redirects.say: Height is the straight up-and-down distance from the base, like a ladder standing on it, not the slanted edge.
misconception_redirects.praise: You measured straight up from the base, that is the real height.

quick_checks.prompt: A triangle has a base of 6 and a height of 5. Area?
quick_checks.look_for: 15 (6 x 5 = 30, then halve). An answer of 30 means the halving was skipped.

quick_checks.prompt: An L-shape is a 4 by 3 rectangle plus a 2 by 2 square. Total area?
quick_checks.look_for: 16 (12 + 4), splitting the figure into two known pieces.

worked_solution.stem: A triangle has a base of 6 cm and a height of 4 cm. What is its area?

steps.annotation: Base times height fills the rectangle the triangle sits in.
The diagonal cuts the rectangle into two equal triangles.
Halve the rectangle's area.
Area is in square units.

faded_example.stem: A triangle has a base of 10 in. and a height of 6 in. What is its area?

steps.annotation: Base times height fills the surrounding rectangle.
The triangle covers half of it.
Divide the rectangle's area by 2.
State the triangle's area in square units.

sentence_starters: The rectangle holds ___ squares, so the triangle holds half: ___.
I split the figure into ___ and ___, then added the areas.
The height is ___ because it goes straight up from the base.

skills.name: Evaluate a formula by substituting a value for the variable

prerequisite_skill.description: Substitute a number for a variable in an expression or formula, including squaring, and evaluate it in the right order.

skills.i_do_script: A formula is a recipe with a blank in it, and substituting means filling the blank with the number, everywhere the letter appears. Watch: P = 2l + 2w with l = 6 and w = 4. I rewrite the formula with the numbers in the blanks: 2 x 6 + 2 x 4. Multiply first, then add: 12 + 8 = 20. One more: s squared, written s^2, with s = 7 means 7 x 7 = 49, not 7 x 2. Substitute first, write the full expression, then follow the order of operations.

canonical_error.pattern: Evaluates a squared variable by doubling instead of multiplying the number by itself
canonical_error.example: For s^2 with s = 7, writes 14 (7 x 2) instead of 49 (7 x 7)
canonical_error.why: The student reads the exponent 2 as times 2. The exponent counts how many times the number is used as a factor: s^2 means s times s.

skills.item_template: An expression or measurement formula with one or two variables, whole-number or simple decimal values, exponents no higher than 2. Student substitutes and evaluates. Numeric response.

sample_items.stem: Evaluate 3n when n = 5.
Evaluate 2l + 2w when l = 6 and w = 4.
Evaluate s^2 when s = 7.
The formula P = 4s gives the perimeter of a square. Find P when s = 9.
Evaluate 6a when a = 2.5.
Evaluate n^2 when n = 10.
The formula A = l x w gives the area of a rectangle. Find A when l = 8 and w = 3.
Evaluate 2x + 3 when x = 6.

redirect_script.stop: Did you replace the letter with the number everywhere it appears?
redirect_script.prompt: Rewrite the formula with the number sitting in every blank the letter left. Then evaluate in order: exponents, then multiply, then add. Remember s^2 means s times itself.
redirect_script.praise: You substituted first and then followed the order, that is how formulas work.

vocabulary.definition: A letter that holds the place of a number in an expression or formula.
Replace a variable with its number everywhere it appears.
Work out the value of an expression after substituting.

worked_example_script.text: Write P = 2l + 2w on the board with l = 6 and w = 4. Draw a 6 by 4 rectangle underneath and label all four sides.
Where does the 6 go in the formula? Where does the 4 go?
Substitute: P = 2 x 6 + 2 x 4. Multiply first: 12 + 8. Add: P = 20. Check against the picture: 6 + 4 + 6 + 4 around the rectangle is also 20.
If a student writes 2 x 6 + 2 x 4 = 2 x 10 = 20 by luck or adds left to right as 12 + 2 = 14 x 4, slow down the order: multiply both pairs first, then add.
Your turn: evaluate A = s^2 when s = 5. Is that 5 x 2 or 5 x 5?

practice_problems.stem: Evaluate 4s when s = 3.
Evaluate n + 7 when n = 5.
Evaluate 2l + 2w when l = 7 and w = 3.
Evaluate s^2 when s = 8.
Evaluate 3.14 x d when d = 10.
Evaluate 5n - 2 when n = 4.
The formula A = b x h / 2 gives a triangle's area. Find A when b = 6 and h = 9.
Mia evaluated s^2 when s = 9. Find her mistake and fix it.
practice_problems.answer: She read the exponent as times 2. Squaring means 9 times itself: 9 x 9 = 81.

activities.title: Build the Square, Then the Formula
materials: Formula cards: A = s^2 with different s values
activities.instructions:
1. Draw a formula card, like A = s^2 with s = 4.
2. Build the actual square with tiles: 4 rows of 4. Count the tiles (16).
3. Write the substitution next to the build: 4^2 = 4 x 4 = 16, and check it matches the tile count.
4. Try s = 5 and s = 6. Ask: would s x 2 ever match the tile count?
5. Say each time: the exponent builds a square, it does not double.

activities.title: Formula Fill-In Match
materials: Card deck: formula-with-values cards and value cards
activities.instructions:
1. Spread the cards face up.
2. Match each formula card, like 2l + 2w with l = 5 and w = 2, to its value card.
3. To claim a match, show the substituted expression out loud before the answer.
4. Two decoy value cards come from doubling instead of squaring; set them aside and explain the error.

strategy_links.why: Building s^2 with tiles makes the exponent a picture, a square of tiles, before the rule is stated.
Thinking aloud 'replace the letter, write the whole expression, then evaluate in order' makes the invisible substitution step audible.
The doubling-instead-of-squaring error is predictable and worth confronting directly in worked examples.

questioning_prompts: What number replaces the letter, and where does it go?
Did you rewrite the whole expression before evaluating?
What does the exponent 2 tell you to do?
Which operation comes first here, and why?
How could you check your value against a picture of the shape?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student evaluates s^2 by multiplying by 2.
misconception_redirects.say: Build it with tiles: s^2 is a square, s rows of s tiles. For s = 7 that is 7 x 7 = 49, and 14 would only be two rows.
misconception_redirects.praise: You multiplied the number by itself, that is squaring.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student substitutes for one variable but leaves the other as a letter, or drops a term.
misconception_redirects.say: Every letter gets its number. Rewrite the whole formula with numbers in every blank before you compute anything.
misconception_redirects.praise: You filled every blank first, so the arithmetic was straightforward.

quick_checks.look_for: 25 (5 x 5). An answer of 10 means the exponent was read as times 2.

worked_solution.stem: Evaluate P = 2l + 2w when l = 6 and w = 4.

steps.annotation: Start from the formula with its blanks.
Substitute: 6 for every l, 4 for every w.
Multiply first, following the order of operations.
Add. Check: 6 + 4 + 6 + 4 around the rectangle is also 20.

faded_example.stem: Evaluate P = 2l + 2w when l = 9 and w = 5.

steps.annotation: Start from the formula.
Substitute 9 for l and 5 for w.
Multiply both pairs.
Add and state P.

sentence_starters: I replaced ___ with ___ everywhere it appears.
The exponent 2 means ___ times itself, so ___^2 = ___.

skills.name: Calculate the circumference of a circle given the radius or diameter
skills.i_do_script: Pi is a measured fact before it's a formula: wrap a string around any circular lid, then lay that string along the lid's diameter -- it fits a little more than 3 times, every lid, every size. That 'a little more than 3' is pi, about 3.14, and it's WHY the circumference formula is C = pi d: the distance around is always pi diameters. If I'm given the radius instead, the diameter is twice it, so the same formula wears a second form: C = 2 pi r. Watch, radius 5: C = 2 pi (5) = 10 pi, about 31.42. Given the diameter 10 instead: C = pi (10) = 10 pi -- same circle, same answer. The trap: a DIAMETER of 10 dropped into 2 pi r as if it were the radius doubles the answer. Sanity check every result against the meaning: the distance around is just over 3 diameters.

canonical_error.pattern: Uses the diameter in place of the radius in C = 2πr, doubling the circumference
canonical_error.example: Given a diameter of 10, computes 2π(10) = 20π instead of πd = 10π (or 2π(5) = 10π)
canonical_error.why: The student grabs the number in the problem and drops it into 2πr without checking whether it is the radius or the diameter. If a diameter is given, either halve it first or use C = πd.

skills.item_template: A radius or diameter is given in text; the student finds the circumference in terms of π or rounded. Numeric response.

sample_items.stem: A circle has a radius of 5 cm. What is the circumference in terms of π?
sample_items.distractor_logic: C = 2π(5) = 10π. Using the area formula gives 25π; forgetting the 2 gives 5π.

sample_items.stem: A circle has a diameter of 10 cm. What is the circumference in terms of π?
sample_items.distractor_logic: C = πd = π(10) = 10π. Treating 10 as the radius gives 20π.

sample_items.stem: A circle has a radius of 3 ft. What is the circumference? Round to the nearest hundredth.
sample_items.distractor_logic: 2π(3) = 6π ≈ 18.85. Using area πr² gives 28.27.

sample_items.stem: A circle has a diameter of 14 in. What is the circumference in terms of π?
sample_items.distractor_logic: C = πd = 14π. Doubling the diameter (2π·14) gives 28π.

redirect_script.stop: Is that number the radius or the diameter?
redirect_script.prompt: Check against the meaning first: the distance around is a bit more than 3 diameters -- does your answer fit that? Check what you were given. If it's the radius, use C = 2πr. If it's the diameter, use C = πd (don't double it). When in doubt, find the radius first.
redirect_script.praise: You matched the formula to what you were given — radius with 2πr, diameter with πd.

vocabulary.definition: The distance all the way around a circle.
The number of times a circle's diameter fits around it, about 3.14.

worked_example_script.text: Hold up a circular lid. Wrap a string once around its rim, then lay the string straight along the diameter, marking off how many diameters fit.
How many diameters did the string cover -- a little more than how many? Would a bigger lid change that count?
Every circle's rim is a little more than 3 diameters -- exactly pi of them. That IS the formula: C = pi d, and since d = 2r, also C = 2 pi r.
Write 'A circle has a radius of 6 m. Find the circumference in terms of π.'
Do you have the radius or the diameter? Which form of the formula fits?
Radius, so C = 2πr = 2π(6) = 12π meters (about 37.70).
If a student writes 6π, ask 'did you use 2πr, or just πr? Circumference with a radius needs the 2.'
Your turn: a circle has a diameter of 8 cm. Find the circumference in terms of π.

practice_problems.stem: A circle gives you its radius. Which circumference formula do you use?
A circle has a radius of 5 m. Circumference in terms of π?
A circle has a diameter of 10 cm. Circumference in terms of π?
A circle has a radius of 3 ft. Circumference to the nearest hundredth?
practice_problems.notes: Decimal rounding with the full value of π.

practice_problems.stem: Kayla found the circumference of a circle with a diameter of 12 in. Find and fix her mistake.
practice_problems.answer: Kayla used the diameter as the radius. With a diameter, use C = πd = π(12) = 12π in. (or halve first: r = 6, 2π(6) = 12π).
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: diameter used as radius, doubling the circumference.

practice_problems.stem: A circle has a diameter of 20 m. Circumference to the nearest hundredth?
A circle's circumference is 16π. Give a radius and a diameter that produce it.
One circle has a radius of 8; another has a diameter of 8. Which has the larger circumference, and how many times larger?
practice_problems.answer: Radius 8 gives 16π; diameter 8 gives 8π. The radius-8 circle is twice as large.
practice_problems.notes: Explain-why contrast of r versus d.

activities.title: The Lid Lab: Measure Pi
materials: 3-4 circular lids or cans of different sizes
activities.instructions:
1. Each group measures two lids: string around the rim for C, ruler across the middle for d. Record both in cm.
2. Compute C divided by d for every lid and add each result to a class table on the board.
3. Look down the column: big lids, small lids -- what number does C/d keep landing near?
4. Debrief: that constant IS pi. Write C/d = pi, so C = pi d. Where does C = 2 pi r come from?
5. Keep the class table posted -- when a circumference answer looks off, check it against 'a bit more than 3 diameters.'

activities.title: Which Circumference Form?
materials: Card set of 8 circles described by a radius or a diameter
activities.instructions:
1. Sort each card into 'Use C = 2πr' (radius given) or 'Use C = πd' (diameter given).
2. For each card, write the circumference in terms of π.
3. Watch for cards that give a diameter — do NOT double it.
4. Debrief: how did you decide which form to use?

activities.title: Doubled the Diameter
activities.instructions:
1. Read Kayla's circumference for a circle with a diameter of 12.
2. Ask: did she treat 12 as the radius or the diameter?
3. Redo it two ways — with C = πd, and by halving to the radius first.
4. Write the rule for what to do when a diameter is given.

content.error_step: Kayla put the diameter 12 into 2πr as if it were the radius.
content.why: With a diameter, use C = πd = 12π, or halve to r = 6 and use 2π(6) = 12π.

strategy_links.why: The diameter-as-radius error is precise and baitable; find-and-fix with a size check targets it directly.
Thinking aloud 'is this the radius or the diameter, and which form fits?' models the check students skip.
Wrapping a string around a circular lid and measuring makes 'circumference is the distance around' concrete before the formula.

questioning_prompts: Is the number you were given the radius or the diameter?
Which form fits — C = 2πr or C = πd?
Did you remember the 2 in 2πr?
Should the circumference be a little more than 3 times the diameter? Is yours?
How could you check by finding the radius first?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student plugs a diameter into 2πr as if it were the radius.
misconception_redirects.say: Check what you were given. If it's the radius, use C = 2πr. If it's the diameter, use C = πd (don't double it). When in doubt, find the radius first.
misconception_redirects.praise: You matched the formula to what you were given — radius with 2πr, diameter with πd.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student uses πr (forgets the 2) for circumference from a radius.
misconception_redirects.say: Circumference from a radius needs the 2: C = 2πr, not πr. πr would only be half the way around.
misconception_redirects.praise: You kept the 2 in 2πr — that's the full distance around.

quick_checks.prompt: A circle has a radius of 10 cm. Circumference in terms of π?
quick_checks.look_for: 20π (2π·10). An answer of 10π means the student forgot the 2 or used πr.

quick_checks.prompt: A circle has a diameter of 10 cm. Circumference in terms of π?
quick_checks.look_for: 10π (πd). An answer of 20π means the diameter was used as the radius.

sentence_starters: I was given the ___, so I use C = ___.
The circumference is ___π, which is about ___.

worked_solution.stem: A circle has a radius of 6 m. What is the circumference in terms of π?

steps.annotation: Check first — is 6 a radius or a diameter? It's the radius.
Radius given, so use the 2πr form (keep the 2).
2 x 6 = 12; keep π for the exact answer (≈ 37.70).
A little over 3 times the diameter of 12 — reasonable.

faded_example.stem: A circle has a diameter of 14 in. What is the circumference in terms of π?

steps.annotation: A diameter is given, so use C = πd (don't double it).

skills.name: Investigate how changing the radius affects circumference and area
skills.i_do_script: This is the 'above' move: reasoning about HOW circumference and area respond when the radius changes. Because circumference is 2πr (radius to the first power), doubling the radius DOUBLES the circumference. Because area is πr² (radius squared), doubling the radius QUADRUPLES the area — it grows by the square of the scale factor. Watch: radius 5 gives area 25π; radius 10 gives area 100π, which is 4 times as big, not 2. Multi-step problems also chain the formulas: a wheel's circumference times the number of rotations gives the distance it rolls.

canonical_error.pattern: Assumes doubling the radius doubles the area (treating area as linear like circumference)
canonical_error.example: Says a radius-10 circle has twice the area of a radius-5 circle (50π), instead of four times (100π vs 25π)
canonical_error.why: The student applies the circumference intuition (double the radius, double the result) to area, but area depends on r², so it scales by the SQUARE of the factor: doubling gives 2² = 4 times.

skills.item_template: A multi-part scenario: compute circumference/area for two radii and compare, or chain circumference with rotations. Multi-part response.

sample_items.stem: A circle has a radius of 5 cm. Part A: area in terms of π? Part B: if the radius doubles to 10 cm, what is the new area, and how many times larger is it?

sample_items.distractor_logic: π(5²) = 25π; π(10²) = 100π; ratio 4. Answering '2 times' treats area as linear.

sample_items.stem: A bicycle tire has a diameter of 22 in. Part A: circumference to the nearest hundredth? Part B: how far does it travel in 15 full rotations? Round to the nearest hundredth.

sample_items.answer: Part A: 64π sq in. Part B: 39π sq in. (64π − 25π).
sample_items.distractor_logic: Outer 64π, inner 25π, ring 39π. Forgetting to subtract the inner gives 64π.

vocabulary.definition: The number the radius is multiplied by; the area grows by its square.

worked_example_script.text: Write 'A circle's radius grows from 3 to 6. What happens to the area?'
What is the area at radius 3? At radius 6? How many times bigger?
π(3²) = 9π and π(6²) = 36π. 36π ÷ 9π = 4, so the area quadruples.
If a student says 'it doubles,' ask 'the radius doubled, but area uses r² — what is 2 squared?'
Your turn: a radius goes from 4 to 8. By what factor does the area grow?

diagnostic_flow.description: Start with S5, a real-world circle problem, the At-proficiency workhorse where the student must choose circumference or area. If they pass, push to S6 (how changing the radius affects circumference and area). If they fail, drop below grade level: B1 checks grade 6 area by decomposing (triangles, parallelograms, composite figures) and B2 checks evaluating a formula by substitution, the two skills the circle formulas lean on. If those wobble, the foundations F1 (perimeter as adding side lengths) and F2 (area as rows of unit squares) locate the gap in grades 3 to 5. S1 through S4 remain available to probe the standard's own forward and reverse formula work.
